newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's land radicals march into capital.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's land radicals march into capital.

text.p: Landless peasants marched into the Brazilian capital on Thursday to the cheers of more than 25,000 demonstrators in the biggest protest faced by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.

The demonstrators opposed to Cardoso's pro-market reforms braved a rainstorm to cheer the 1,500 peasants of the Landless Movement (MST) as they filed into Brasilia's massive Ministries Esplanade after a 750-mile (1,200 km) march to demand land and justice for slain colleagues.

"Comrades, do not give in. We can still dream of a better future," MST leader Joao Pedro Stedile urged protestors waving red flags as left-wing luminaries, trade union leaders and liberal Catholic bishops jostled for space behind him.
The MST has emerged as a new left-wing force in Brazil that has captured the imagination of the public with its high-profile tactic of invading and cultivating unused farmland.
Stedile said the MST would defy calls from the government to give up the occupations which often lead to violence.
"There will be more and more occupations. We don't expect the government to carry out proper land reform program as an act of generosity," Stedile said.
Brazil has one of the world's worst land distribution ratios, with about half arable land in the hands of just two percent of landowners.

The struggle for land ownership is also one of the main factors behind Brazil's soaring levels of violence. More than 100 people have been killed in land disputes since Cardoso took office in January 1995.

Thursday's protest marked the first anniversary of the killing by police of 19 peasants demanding land. The massacre heaped criticism from international rights groups on Brazil and spurred Cardoso to declare land reform a priority.
No one has been arrested for that killing, despite television pictures clearly showing police officers firing machineguns indiscriminately into the crowd of protestors.

The MST also says steps taken by the government after the massacre to speed up land reform, provide more credit to settlers and raise taxes on unused farmland have failed to stem the growing number of families seeking land.
Cardoso, whose popularity remains high but is increasingly under fire for failing to match low inflation with improved social conditions, defended his record on land reform.

"In my government I have settled more people than in any other period of Brazilian history. We have disappropriated 3.4 million hectares, that's the size of Belgium," the president said in an interview with Globo television.

Cardoso was due to meet with MST leaders on Friday, the first top-level meeting between the government and the movement since August last year. "If we join our hands then we will be able to settle more people," Cardoso said.
The president also came under attack on Thursday from the Catholic Church for his economic policies.
"The impoverishment of the people cannot be accepted as the inevitable price of economic development," Brazil's National Bishops Conference (CNBB) said in a statement.

The document called for the suspension of the upcoming $5 billion privatization of mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce and criticized lawmakers for setting a $10,000 cap on their monthly income while millions of workers surive on a minimum wage of $105.

In their statement, the bishops urged the government to reconsider its economic development model and called for the adoption of a far-reaching agrarian reform program and policies to provide housing and eradicate illiteracy and hunger.
